opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. That paper, which I wrote with Aaron Mueller, came out of a longer-running question in my lab: what does it take for a learner to generalize the way humans do when the data are ambiguous between a hierarchical rule and a simpler linear one?

The classic test case is question formation in English. Take "The dog that is sleeping is happy." To make a question, you move the main-clause auxiliary: "Is the dog that is sleeping happy?" A learner could, in principle, get by with a linear rule like "move the first auxiliary." That works for most simple sentences children hear, but it gives you the wrong answer for sentences like this one. Humans reliably go with the hierarchical rule, and this has long been one of the central arguments for innate structural biases.

So we asked what properties of a neural language model push it toward the hierarchical generalization. We looked at two kinds of factors: the training data, and the architecture.

On the architecture side, the clearest finding concerned depth. If you hold the number of parameters roughly constant and trade width for depth, deeper models were more likely to generalize hierarchically than shallower, wider ones. That makes some intuitive sense: hierarchical structure involves composing representations in a nested way, and depth gives the model more opportunities for that kind of stepwise composition. I wouldn't call it a clean architectural prior for syntax, though. It's more that some configurations make the hierarchical solution easier to find than the shortcut.

The data side turned out to be at least as interesting. Pretraining on simpler, child-directed language actually supported hierarchical generalization better than pretraining on a comparable amount of more complex text like Wikipedia. Models also needed a lot of exposure before the hierarchical preference reliably emerged, much more than children seem to need.

So my overall view is that architecture matters, but not in the sense of "the transformer has syntax built in." Architecture shapes which generalizations are easy to reach, and it interacts with the data. A standard transformer with no explicit structural bias can arrive at hierarchical generalizations, but it isn't strongly predisposed to them, and it takes far more data than a human learner. That gap is what interests me most scientifically. It suggests humans either have stronger inductive biases or learn from richer signals than text, and figuring out which biases close that gap is how these models can actually inform debates about language acquisition.

r001.rationale: The response asks what pushes models toward hierarchical generalization and compares architecture while holding parameter count roughly constant; it also compares training data types using comparable amounts.

r002.rationale: It reports that, at roughly the same parameter count, deeper models were more likely than shallower, wider ones to generalize hierarchically.

r003.rationale: It discusses stronger human inductive biases and the need to identify useful biases, but does not suggest that architectures substantially different from Transformers could improve syntax learning with less data or computation.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short version is that architecture matters a lot more than people tend to assume, and the way it matters is a bit subtle.

The motivation for that paper came from a long-running puzzle. Humans generalize syntactic structure from very little data, and they do it in a hierarchical way. If you show a child a few examples of a question like "Is the dog that is barking hungry?", they figure out that you move the main-clause auxiliary, not just the first auxiliary you come across in the sentence. That's the classic structure-sensitivity result. Standard neural networks, when you train them on comparable amounts of data, tend to go for the linear rule instead, or they land somewhere in between and only sort it out after seeing enormous amounts of text. So the question we asked was: can we build the right structural bias into a model in advance, so it generalizes the way people do, rather than hoping it emerges from scale?

What we did was take syntactic transformations, things like question formation and passivization, and pretrain a model on an auxiliary task that essentially teaches it to pay attention to constituency structure before it ever sees the target task. Then we fine-tuned on the actual transformation with a small amount of data and asked how it generalized to the structurally ambiguous cases.

The finding that I think is most interesting is that the inductive bias really does get planted. A model that has been exposed to tree structure in that way, even indirectly, will pick the hierarchical generalization from a handful of examples, whereas a standard transformer trained the same way on the same amount of data just doesn't. And it transfers across different transformations, which suggests it's not learning a trick for one construction but something closer to a general preference for structure.

So how do I see the role of architecture? I'd put it this way. The architecture determines what the model finds easy to learn, not just what it's able to learn in principle. A transformer can represent hierarchical structure, we know that, but nothing about it makes hierarchy the default hypothesis. The strong results we see at scale partly reflect the fact that with enough data the hierarchical rule is simply the one that fits, so the model gets there eventually. What that hides is a huge data efficiency gap relative to humans. If you care about that gap, and I do, because I think it's a window into how linguistic knowledge is actually acquired, then you have to think about what biases are built in.

The other thing I'd stress is that "architecture" is broader than the computation graph. Pretraining objectives are part of the architecture in the sense that matters. We didn't change the transformer itself; we changed what it had seen before the real task, and that was enough to shift its generalization behavior. That's a somewhat optimistic result, because it means you don't necessarily need exotic tree-structured networks to get tree-structured biases. You can instill them. The less optimistic reading is that we're still doing this by hand, and we don't have a great story yet for where those biases come from in a model that's just reading text.

r001.rationale: The response discusses architecture, data efficiency, and generalization with the same amount of data, but it does not ask whether architecture affects sentence-structure-based generalization independently of model size or training-data quantity.

r002.rationale: It does not report evidence comparing deeper Transformers with wider, shallower Transformers at the same parameter count.

r003.rationale: It says tree-structured biases can be instilled without exotic tree-structured networks, rather than suggesting substantially different architectures could improve syntactic generalization with less data or computation.

astra-6.text:
I think architecture matters because it gives the model an inductive bias—a preference for certain kinds of generalizations. In syntax, we’re interested in whether a model learns hierarchical relationships, rather than just patterns in the sequence of words. Those can look very similar on the training data and then make different predictions on new sentences.

The idea behind “How to Plant Trees in Language Models” is to give models a bias toward that hierarchical structure and ask what that buys us. You don’t necessarily have to build the entire grammar into the architecture. You can also encourage structure through the way the model is trained.

So I wouldn’t frame the conclusion as ‘a model without explicit trees can’t learn syntax.’ The question is how reliably it learns the right generalization, how much data it needs, and whether that generalization holds up outside the examples it’s seen. Architecture is one way to influence that, alongside the training objective and the data.

r001.rationale: The response discusses architecture’s influence on hierarchical generalization and data needs, but does not address whether that influence is independent of model size or training-data quantity.

r002.rationale: It gives no preliminary evidence comparing deeper Transformers with wider, shallower Transformers at the same parameter count.

r003.rationale: It does not suggest that architectures substantially different from Transformers could achieve stronger syntactic generalization with less data or computation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think architecture matters, but it’s useful to distinguish between what a model can learn and what it’s biased to learn. A sufficiently flexible model might be able to represent syntactic structure, but that doesn’t mean it will discover that structure from the data it receives. It may find a shortcut that works well on the training examples and then fails when you test it on a new construction.

The idea behind “How to Plant Trees in Language Models” is to investigate ways of giving models an inductive bias toward hierarchical structure. Language comes to us as a sequence of words, but the relationships that matter for syntax often involve phrases and their internal organization, rather than just which words are next to one another. If we build some sensitivity to that organization into the model, does it learn more robust generalizations?

That doesn’t necessarily mean hard-coding a complete grammar. The interesting question is how much structure you need to provide, and how much the model can learn for itself. And from a cognitive perspective, that gives us a way to make hypotheses about learning more precise: rather than simply saying that learners need an innate bias, we can implement a particular bias and examine what it actually buys us.

r001.rationale: The response asks whether hierarchical structure improves robust generalization, but does not compare architecture’s effect with model size or training-data quantity.

r002.rationale: It gives no preliminary evidence comparing deeper Transformers with wider, shallower Transformers at equal parameter counts.

r003.rationale: It does not suggest that architectures substantially different from Transformers could generalize syntactically with less data or computation.
